yfinance_call_path_investigation.native_timeout_value: 30s per individual HTTP request (yfinance's own default), YfConfig.network.retries=0 (no internal retry loop)
yfinance_call_path_investigation.why_native_timeout_alone_is_insufficient: resolve_instrument_identity/Ticker.info never exposes a way to override yfinance's own internal 30s-per-call default from our call site, and .info makes SEVERAL sequential internal calls (cookie/crumb negotiation, quoteSummary fetch, v7 quote fetch, a complementary timeseries fetch) -- each independently up to 30s. Worst case (every one times out) is bounded by yfinance's own internals to roughly 120-240s, not literally infinite, but still far above the requested 10-15s target and not directly controllable without wrapping.
yfinance_call_path_investigation.empirical_check: A direct standalone call (yf.Ticker('QQQ').info) completed in 1.07s with 103 keys at the time of this task's investigation -- confirming the fast path is healthy under current conditions; the wrapper below protects the rare/slow/stalled path regardless.

threadpool_naive_approach_rejected.what_broke: A first implementation used `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4, ...)` as a module-level singleton, never explicitly shut down, with `future.result(timeout=N)` bounding the caller. This own task's OWN test suite hung past a 60s harness timeout when exercised.
threadpool_naive_approach_rejected.root_cause_of_the_hang: concurrent.futures.thread registers a process-exit atexit hook (`_python_exit`) that JOINS every worker thread of EVERY ThreadPoolExecutor ever created, unconditionally, at interpreter shutdown -- regardless of whether the caller's own `future.result(timeout=...)` already gave up on that task. A genuinely-stuck task (this task's own 'never returns' test fake, and by extension a truly-stalled Yahoo Finance connection) would hang the ENTIRE PROCESS at exit, not just the one call.
threadpool_naive_approach_rejected.how_it_was_diagnosed: Isolated by running individual tests (all passed quickly) versus the full test file together (hung); confirmed via a minimal standalone repro outside pytest that a single hanging call bounded correctly and exited cleanly, versus multiple tests accumulating stuck ThreadPoolExecutor workers exhausting the pool for later tests. This is documented in detail as a deliberate lesson in the _DaemonThreadPool docstring in agent_utils.py.
threadpool_naive_approach_rejected.conclusion: future.result(timeout=...) alone bounds the CALLER's wait, but does not bound PROCESS shutdown if the underlying mechanism is ThreadPoolExecutor. A different mechanism was required.

selected_bounding_mechanism.design: _DaemonThreadPool: a small, custom, fixed-size (max_workers=4) worker pool built on plain threading.Thread(daemon=True) workers pulling from a queue.Queue, each submission returning a standard concurrent.futures.Future.

why_this_satisfies_preference_order.A_native_http_timeout: Available (yfinance's own 30s default) but not independently overridable from this call site without monkeypatching yfinance internals -- rejected as too invasive for a best-effort, non-critical lookup.
why_this_satisfies_preference_order.B_project_session_mechanism: No project-level HTTP session wrapper with a configurable deadline exists for this specific yfinance call path.
why_this_satisfies_preference_order.C_isolatable_mechanism: Selected. Daemon threads are abandoned (not joined) at interpreter exit -- Python's atexit machinery only tracks and joins ThreadPoolExecutor-created (non-daemon) threads, never daemon threads created directly. A fixed-size pool (not one new thread per call) additionally guarantees no unbounded thread growth under repeated timeouts.

selected_bounding_mechanism.not_a_permanently_leaking_thread_as_the_: On the fast, common path (empirically ~0.26-1.1s), no thread is ever left running -- the worker completes and returns to the pool immediately. Only a genuinely-stalled call (rare, and itself bounded by yfinance's own ~30-240s internal ceiling in real production use) leaves one of the 4 fixed workers busy until it eventually resolves on its own.

selected_timeout_value.justification: Within the requested 10-15s target range. The lookup is best-effort, non-critical, and already fail-open by design (docstring: 'if yfinance is unavailable, rate-limited, or doesn't recognise the ticker, we return {} and the caller falls back to ticker-only context'). 12s comfortably exceeds the empirically-observed healthy-path latency (~0.26-1.1s in this task's own live run and standalone test) by more than an order of magnitude -- essentially zero risk of false-positive timeout on a normal call -- while capping the worst case at roughly 1.3% of the ~903s previously observed across three independent live-run failures.
selected_timeout_value.exposed_as: An internal module-level constant (_INSTRUMENT_IDENTITY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) in tradingagents/agents/utils/agent_utils.py, consistent with this project's existing pattern for internal, non-user-facing bounds (e.g. week2_llm.py's DEFAULT_*_CONCURRENCY constants) -- no new user-facing configuration was introduced, per instruction.

real_wall_clock_bound_proof.method: A fake lookup (_never_returns) genuinely blocks forever via threading.Event().wait() with no timeout on the wait itself -- it can never return on its own. The test measures WALL-CLOCK elapsed time of the resolve_instrument_identity(...) CALL itself (not merely whether a TimeoutError was raised internally), using a 0.15s test-mode timeout, and asserts elapsed < timeout + 1.0s.
real_wall_clock_bound_proof.measured_elapsed_in_this_run: 0.156s against a configured 0.15s bound (test); 0.155s against the same bound in a standalone non-pytest reproduction used to diagnose the ThreadPoolExecutor issue.
real_wall_clock_bound_proof.proves: The caller's return is genuinely, measurably bounded -- not merely a caught-and-ignored TimeoutError while the caller silently waits longer.
